headline: Cameras film three snow leopards in Chatkal hills; herders still have no compensation
dek: The Ilbirs Station says one early-morning sequence is not a count, and neither it nor the Ministry of Natural Resources sets payment for lost sheep and goats.
paragraphs: The Ilbirs Station at Uuk-Bulak released footage this week from a line of camera traps in the Chatkal Highlands. It shows three snow leopards crossing a snow-dusted scree slope in a single early-morning sequence. The station's head said the animals may be a female with two grown young. She added that the footage cannot show it.

"This is one sequence, not a count," Dr Aizhan Torobekova, who heads the station, told the Herald. "Three cats on one slope at one hour tells us three cats were there. It does not tell us how many live in these hills, or whether they are related." She said the team would need further seasons of images, and tracks and other field signs, before saying anything about numbers.

IradOne reported the footage on Wednesday, and the government said in a statement the same day that the cameras had recorded the animals. Neither account says who pays when the cats take livestock, and the answer is the same today as in the Herald's 6 November report from Besh-Tash: nobody has published a scheme.

The station, in Sary-Bulak District, opened on 23 October. It is run by the Faculty of Biology and Chemistry of Talas State University with vets from the Talas Veterinary Research Center. Dr Torobekova said the camera line stands on tribal hill pasture and runs only with the agreement of the clan councils. Releases of animals into the Chatkal hills follow the same rule.

Herders in the hills and in Toktogul District have asked again whether any compensation exists. Asylbek Kenjegul uulu, a herder in Toktogul District, said he had lost sheep to cats in two of the past four winters and had never been told whom to ask. "People say the cats are Irad's pride, and I do not argue," he said. "But the sheep were mine, and a hay bill is not paid with pride." Hay in the valleys is 26 som a bale today.

Asked who answers for such losses, Dr Torobekova said the station does not set compensation. "We study the animals and treat injured ones. Payment to herders is a decision for the ministry, and for the clan councils where the pasture is theirs." The Ministry of Natural Resources, which was represented at the station's opening, has published no compensation scheme. Asked by the Herald whether one was being drafted, the ministry had not replied by the time this edition went to press.

The question stays open in part because the cats move across land that belongs to different authorities. The cameras sit on tribal pasture, outside the ISEZ line. The ministry's writ runs only on the ISEZ side, and any payment to herders in the hills would need the councils' consent.

Dr Torobekova said the team will collect the memory cards again after the winter snow settles, and that any further footage will be shared with the clan councils as well as the ministry. Mr Kenjegul uulu said the herders would wait for that. "We would like an answer before the lambing, not after."
